candidates.title: ZWINT promotes DLBCL progression by modulating CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity
candidates.abstract: Background ZWINT (ZW10 interacting kinetochore protein), a core component of the kinetochore complex, plays a role in maintaining genomic stability. Although elevated ZWINT expression correlates with tumor progression and poor prognosis in various cancers, its functions and molecular mechanisms in DLBCL remain unclear. Methods ZWINT expression and clinical relevance were evaluated in DLBCL cohorts and validated in patient tissues and cell lines. Cell proliferation, apoptosis, and chromosomal stability were assessed in vitro following shRNA-mediated ZWINT knockdown. Syngeneic murine lymphoma models were utilized to examine tumor progression, immune cell infiltration, CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity, and synergy with anti-PD-1 blockade. Results ZWINT was significantly upregulated in DLBCL tissues and cell lines, with elevated expression associated with adverse clinicopathological features and shorter overall survival. Functionally, ZWINT knockdown suppressed cell proliferation, promoted apoptosis, and inhibited tumor growth. Notably, its antitumor effects were more pronounced in immunocompetent BALB/c mice than in immunodeficient NOG mice, suggesting the involvement of host immunity. Mechanistically, ZWINT depletion increased chromosomal instability and DNA damage, accompanied by molecular changes consistent with cGAS-STING/type I interferon (IFN) signaling activation, enhanced MHC-I, PD-L1, and chemokine expression. Consequently, ZWINT knockdown augmented intratumoral CD8 + T cell infiltration, increased cytotoxic effector molecules, alleviated T-cell exhaustion, and sensitized lymphomas to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy. Conclusion Our findings establish ZWINT as a key oncogenic driver and adverse prognostic factor in DLBCL. ZWINT knockdown enhances antitumor efficacy through driving cell-intrinsic apoptosis and promoting CD8 + T cell-mediated antitumor immunity via the chromosomal instability-associated cGAS-STING signaling pathway, offering a promising strategy to improve sensitivity to ICB.

candidates.title: Differential effects of Pseudomonas fluorescens and Trichoderma harzianum combined with water-soluble amino acid fertilizer on rhizosphere reassembly and tobacco growth
candidates.abstract: Long-term monocropping and excessive fertilization have degraded soil function and intensified soil-borne disease, constraining tobacco productivity. Functional microbial inoculants represent a promising strategy for soil remediation, yet the mechanisms by which beneficial microorganisms reconstruct rhizosphere microecosystems and interact with soil nutrients remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of Pseudomonas fluorescens (Ps), Trichoderma harzianum (Tr), and their combined application with water-soluble amino acid fertilizer (PsA and TrA) on tobacco growth, soil properties, and rhizosphere microbial community. All inoculant treatments significantly reduced the incidence of soil-borne diseases, promoted tobacco growth, and improved soil nutrient availability, with PsA and TrA showing particularly strong effects. Compared with the control, PsA reduced bacterial wilt incidence by 34.30%, while TrA reduced root rot incidence by 54.24%. Tobacco leaf area increased by 15.63%, 23.97%, 27.16%, and 41.13% under Ps, PsA, Tr, and TrA treatments, respectively. Soil organic matter content increased by 4.32–17.75% across the inoculant treatments. Ps and PsA increased bacterial α-diversity, reshaped bacterial community composition, enriched potential beneficial genera including Gemmatimonas and Flavisolibacter , and reduced the OTU number of potential pathogenic Ralstonia compared with CK group. Moreover, Tr and TrA restructured fungal community, reduced the relative abundance of potential pathogenic Setophoma and optimized fungal ecological networks by decreasing negative cohesion and promoting potential keystone taxon such as Mortierella . Taxonomically based predictions indicated that Ps was associated with bacterial chemoheterotrophy and aerobic chemoheterotrophy, while Tr was associated with predicted fungal guilds related to plant and wood saprotrophy, respectively. SEM suggested potential associations linking Pseudomonas and Trichoderma abundance, microbial community properties, soil nutrients, and tobacco growth traits. The addition of amino acid fertilizer further strengthened microbial functionality and yield promotion. These findings provide new insights into amino acid-assisted microbial ecological regulation and highlight the potential of combining functional microbial inoculants with nutrient amendments for sustainable tobacco production.

candidates.title: SvCmr1-mediated regulation of melanin and Altersolanol A biosynthesis governs virulence in Stemphylium vesicarium
candidates.abstract: Stemphylium vesicarium is a destructive necrotrophic pathogen that causes leaf blight and severe yield losses in multiple crops. The polyketide phytotoxin Altersolanol A acts as a key virulence factor of this fungus. Although the polyketide synthase SvPKS1 catalyzes Altersolanol A biosynthesis, the upstream regulatory mechanism governing Altersolanol A production remains poorly understood. Here, we functionally characterized SvCMR1, a conserved chimeric zinc-finger transcription factor harboring both Zn 2 Cys 6 and C 2 H 2 domains. This transcription factor localizes to the nucleus and exhibits transcriptional activation activity. Deletion of SvCmr1 markedly reduced the biosynthesis of melanin and Altersolanol A, and substantially attenuated fungal virulence. Transcriptomic and RT-qPCR analyses revealed that SvCMR1 positively regulates DHN-melanin biosynthetic genes but has no effect on SvPks1 . Tricyclazole inhibition and exogenous 1,8-DHN supplementation assays support a functional association between the DHN-melanin pathway and Altersolanol A biosynthesis. Collectively, SvCMR1 serves as a regulator coordinating melanin and Altersolanol A biosynthesis, together with fungal virulence. These findings deepen our mechanistic understanding of S. vesicarium pathogenicity and provide valuable insights for the sustainable control of Stemphylium leaf blight.

candidates.title: Single-cell transcriptomic profiling identifies a proliferative ATAD2+ tumor cell state with MYBL1 as a predicted regulator in osteosarcoma
candidates.abstract: Background Osteosarcoma is aggressive. It metastasizes early, and current therapy often fails. Tumor cells (TCs) come in many functional states. Their interplay with immune and stromal cells shapes a microenvironment that favors tumor growth. Which TC state drives malignant progression, immune escape, and microenvironmental control is still unclear. This uncertainty limits precision immunotherapy. Methods We integrated two publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, and conducted unsupervised clustering, copy number variation inference, and trajectory analysis to characterize cellular heterogeneity. Next, functional enrichment analysis, CellChat, and SCENIC were performed to investigate intercellular communication networks and transcription factor regulatory landscapes. We then tested whether MYBL1 contributes to these phenotypes by silencing it in Saos-2 and U2OS cells; knockdown effects were measured with CCK-8 assays for proliferation, colony formation for clonogenicity, Transwell chambers for migration, and Annexin V/PI staining with flow cytometry for apoptosis. Results Single-cell analysis resolved osteosarcoma tumor cells into seven transcriptionally defined clusters/states. One of them, C4 ATAD2 + , stood out. Its programs centered on the cell cycle and DNA replication, and most of its cells sat in S phase. CellChat predicted enriched SLIT- and UNC5-related ligand–receptor interactions. SCENIC predicted MYBL1 as a candidate transcriptional regulator of this subtype. Knocking MYBL1 down in osteosarcoma cells slowed proliferation and migration, cut colony formation, and raised apoptosis. Conclusion We defined the single-cell-resolution characterization of high-risk TC populations in osteosarcoma and found that C4 ATAD2 + TCs represented a proliferative state associated with MYBL1, with predicted communication through the SLIT and UNC5 signaling pathways. The TC state highlighted in this study was associated with predicted cell–cell communication in the tumor ecosystem, while the MYBL1-associated regulatory network and the SLIT and UNC5 signaling pathways may serve as candidate targets for future study.

candidates.title: Development of Catalytically Inactive APOBEC3A Variants with Enhanced Thermal Stability and Expression Yield
candidates.abstract: Abstract APOBEC3A (A3A) is a single-stranded (ss) DNA cytidine deaminase implicated in cancer mutagenesis and therapy resistance, making it a compelling cancer target. However, wildtype A3A is toxic to bacteria complicating recombinant protein production. To enable structural and deamination-independent analyses, catalytically inactive variants are often used, most commonly A3A-E72A and A3A-E72Q. We previously showed that the E72Q substitution destabilizes the enzyme, reducing thermal stability and ssDNA binding compared to an alanine substitution. Here, we applied nonequilibrium alchemical free energy calculations to identify stabilizing substitutions at the catalytic residue, which predicted hydrophobic substitutions such as E72V. Based on this analysis, E72V, E72G, and E72M were selected for experimental validation and evaluated for thermal stability, ssDNA binding affinity, secondary structure percentage, and propensity to unfold and aggregate. Consistent with alchemical predictions, E72V maintained thermal stability, ssDNA binding, and folding properties comparable to E72A. Notably, E72V also provided an approximately 2-fold increase in bacterial expression yield while avoiding the substantial batch-to-batch yield variability observed with E72A. The equivalent E255V substitution in the closely related APOBEC3B catalytic domain (A3Bctd) yielded higher thermal stability, comparable ssDNA binding, and an approximately 3-fold improvement in expression yield relative to its alanine counterpart. These results identify A3A-E72V and A3Bctd-E255V as improved catalytically inactive scaffolds and establish a foundation for APOBEC3 protein engineering for crystallographic studies and structure-guided drug development.

candidates.title: Systemic IgA responses elicited by full-length MSP1 vaccination drive myeloid effector responses and are influenced by prior malaria exposure
candidates.abstract: Introduction Although IgG is well established as a mediator of malaria immunity, the role of systemic IgA following malaria vaccination remains poorly understood. As the second most abundant serum antibody isotype, IgA mediates distinct effector functions on myeloid cells. We investigated the magnitude, kinetics, and functional properties of IgA induced by a full-length recombinant Plasmodium falciparum MSP1 vaccine formulated with GLA-SE adjuvant in individuals with different malaria exposure histories. Methods MSP1-specific IgA responses were assessed longitudinally in malaria-naïve and semi-immune adults following vaccination. IgA-enriched preparations were evaluated for parasite recognition and exploratory functional activity, including antibody-dependent respiratory burst (ADRB), opsonic phagocytosis, NK-cell activation, complement fixation and iC3b formation, and parasite growth inhibition activity (GIA). Anti-MSP1 IgA was also measured in an age-stratified cohort from the Democratic Republic of Congo. Results Vaccination elicited robust MSP1-specific IgA responses in malaria-naïve individuals, peaking 4 weeks after the second vaccine dose. In contrast, semi-immune participants generated significantly lower IgA titers, indicating that prior malaria exposure modulates vaccine-induced IgA responses. IgA-enriched preparations induced strong neutrophil ADRB and enhanced monocyte opsonic phagocytosis. Although IgA did not mediate parasite growth inhibition or C1q fixation, iC3b formation was detected in selected high-titer samples. High pre-existing immunity limited further enhancement of neutrophil activity but did not affect NK-cell activation. In the endemic cohort, anti-MSP1 IgA levels increased progressively with age, suggesting cumulative natural exposure promotes the development of MSP1-specific IgA. Conclusions Full-length MSP1 vaccination induces a functionally distinct IgA response that preferentially triggers myeloid effector responses. The magnitude and functional characteristics of these responses are influenced by prior malaria exposure, underscoring the importance of isotype-specific functional analyses in malaria vaccine development and the evaluation of protective immunity.

candidates.title: Lactic acid bacteria fermentation broth remediates the antibiotic resistome and neutralizes biosafety risks in swine gut
candidates.abstract: Background The widespread dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in livestock farming poses a severe global biosecurity threat, requiring effective non-antibiotic mitigation strategies. Methods This study investigated the impact of a lactic acid bacteria (LAB) fermentation broth on the swine gut resistome, mobilome, and virulome using high-resolution metagenomics. Results The intervention induced a clear quantitative versus qualitative divergence. While total ARG abundance marginally increased due to host-adapted core genotypes [e.g., tet(W) , lnu(C) ], ARG subtype diversity sharply collapsed. Crucially, the intervention accomplished a targeted reduction of critical, clinical-priority ARGs, such as NDM-6 , CTX-M-3 , OXA-72 , and QnrS1 reduced below the detection limit of the metagenomic assay. The fermentation broth also significantly down-regulated the counts and abundances of mobile genetic elements (MGEs) and virulence factors (VFs). Contig-level analysis revealed a physical disentanglement of the ARGs-MGEs-VFs co-occurrence, effectively decoupling the hazardous networks that linked critical ARGs to mobilization vectors ( IS91 , Tn916 ) and pathogenicity traits ( ibcB , nmpc ). Consequently, the comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Risk Index (ARRI) experienced a plunge. Host-tracking analysis confirmed that these plasmid-bound ARGs were exclusively sequestered within beneficial anaerobic commensals (primarily Oscillibacter and Prevotella ) rather than clinical pathogens. Conclusion The LAB fermentation broth serves as an effective ecological barrier that neutralizes public health risks by physically decoupling ARGs from dissemination vehicles and safely locking them inside the commensal microbiome.

candidates.title: Salinity shapes within- and between-host infection dynamics of the oyster pathogen Vibrio aestuarianus.
candidates.abstract: Environmental variability plays a central role in shaping infectious disease dynamics in marine ecosystems, yet the mechanistic basis of its effects on host-pathogen interactions remains largely unresolved. Recurrent adult mortalities of the Pacific oyster (Magallana gigas) are frequently associated with Vibrio aestuarianus subsp. francensis, but the environmental drivers of outbreak dynamics remain poorly understood. Using complementary approaches spanning national surveillance, field monitoring, controlled experiments, and separate bacterial and host transcriptomic analyses, we assessed distinct aspects of the relationship between salinity and disease dynamics. Twelve years of surveillance data showed that V. aestuarianus was more frequently detected at sites classified as variable-salinity environments, while lower salinity was associated with greater oyster mortality during field monitoring in the Thau Lagoon (France). Under controlled conditions, low salinity increased oyster mortality and enhanced transmission by promoting bacterial shedding, viability and relative dominance in seawater. Transcriptomic analyses showed that low salinity induces the expression of metabolic, stress-response, and virulence-associated genes in V. aestuarianus, while high salinity primarily triggers osmotic stress adaptation. Separate transcriptomic analyses revealed that oyster haemocytes exhibited a salinity-dependent shift. Low salinity is associated with metabolically intensive processes whereas higher salinity conditions are characterized by enrichment of immune-related signalling pathways during infection. Together, these complementary datasets support salinity as an important ecological regulator of V. aestuarianus disease dynamics and identify candidate physiological processes that may contribute to the observed phenotypes. Integrating salinity into disease risk assessment may improve prediction and management of oyster mortality under increasing hydrological variability in coastal environments.

candidates.title: Obesity-associated changes in immune cell dynamics during alphavirus infection revealed by single-cell transcriptomic analysis.
candidates.abstract: Obesity alters host immunity, resulting in worse disease outcomes following infection with various pathogens, including arthritogenic alphaviruses. However, the impact of obesity on the functional landscape of immune cells during acute arthritogenic alphavirus infection remains incompletely explored. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to dissect the blood and tissue immune responses to Mayaro virus (MAYV) infection in lean and obese mice. Footpad injection of MAYV caused significant shifts in immune cell populations and induced robust expression of interferon response and proinflammatory cytokine genes and related pathways in both blood and tissue. In MAYV-infected lean mice, single-cell analysis of the footpad response revealed a unique macrophage subset (F4/80 lo MHCII + ) with high expression of interferon-responsive genes that was replaced by an alternative, F4/80 int population in infected obese mice. Macrophages isolated from lean mice had higher levels of inflammatory gene expression. Furthermore, obese macrophages infected with MAYV and CHIKV ex vivo produce an immunoregulatory response (IL-10) compared to lean macrophages that produce a higher pro-inflammatory response (TNF). The stronger inflammatory response in lean macrophages was associated with less severe systemic disease in lean mice. These results provide evidence for the role of a unique population of macrophages that may contribute to the superior capacity of lean mice to control arthritogenic alphavirus infection.IMPORTANCEArthritogenic alphaviruses-including chikungunya, Mayaro, and Ross River viruses-cause chronic, often disabling joint and muscle disease and are expanding into new regions, yet no approved therapies target the disease process itself. Obesity is a known risk factor for more severe outcomes after infection, but the underlying immune mechanisms have been unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that infection drives widespread interferon and inflammatory responses in blood and infected tissue and that obesity specifically alters the macrophage populations present at the infection site. Lean mice mount a highly activated, interferon-driven macrophage response linked to better control of local inflammation, while obese mice instead accumulate a related but less activated population enriched for necroptosis-associated genes and linked to greater tissue damage. These findings identify a specific macrophage subset as a likely contributor to the more severe alphavirus disease seen with obesity and a potential target for future therapies.

candidates.title: Identification of a highly conserved neutralization epitope targeting poxvirus F13/F13L homologs across seven genera of the subfamily Chordopoxvirinae , family Poxviridae .
candidates.abstract: The emergence of the human monkeypox epidemic sparked interest in the development of broadly protective pan-poxvirus vaccines that protect against all members of the Poxviridae family. Here, we describe a B-cell monoclonal antibody (mAb) raised against the lumpy skin disease virus ORF29 protein that demonstrates broad-spectrum cross-binding activity against seven genera in the Chordopoxvirinae subfamily, Poxviridae family. Subsequently, a novel continuous linear and conformational epitope has been systematically identified among poxviruses. Furthermore, alanine-scanning mutagenesis analysis confirmed that five critical amino acids ( 199 IGGVF 203 ) of this novel epitope were highly conserved among poxviruses. Crucially, neutralizing assays revealed that this mAb (ORF29 3C4-2E9 ) retained broad-spectrum binding and cross-neutralizing activity against capripoxvirus and orthopoxvirus infections in vitro . I n vitro antibody internalization and functional assays demonstrated that full-length IgG from ORF29 3C4-2E9 exhibited higher neutralizing potency than that of its corresponding Fab fragment at the initial stage of viral attachment. Finally, mouse challenge experiments demonstrated that passive ORF29 3C4-2E9 transfer and peptide immunization provided cross-protective efficacy against ectromelia virus infection following intranasal injection in vivo . Our research provides experimental evidence for heterosubtypic immunity and demonstrates the feasibility of epitope-based approaches for developing pan-poxvirus vaccines and antiviral drugs. Importance Similar to the COVID-19 pandemic, the recent global outbreak of human monkeypox highlights the critical need for vaccines and therapeutics that offer broad protection against a range of poxviruses. In this study, we comprehensively describe a monoclonal antibody derived from the lumpy skin disease virus that maintains broad cross-reactive binding and neutralizing activity against various poxviruses, including orthopoxviruses (e.g., monkeypox, vaccinia, and ectromelia) and capripoxviruses. Our study identified a highly conserved epitope within the ORF29 protein and its analogs in seven genera in the subfamily Chordopoxvirinae of the Poxviridae family. Our findings provide the first experimental evidence that heterosubtypic immunity can be achieved through epitope-targeted strategies, thereby paving the way for the development of a universally conserved epitope for a broad-spectrum poxvirus vaccine and antiviral drugs.

candidates.title: The Aspergillus fumigatus C2-domain protein SppA is required for septal integrity and alters susceptibility to echinocandins and neutrophil killing during infection
candidates.abstract: Aspergillus fumigatus is a major opportunistic fungal pathogen whose ability to maintain hyphal integrity and withstand host defenses is critical for virulence. Septal pores, which connect hyphal compartments, are dynamically regulated to preserve cellular integrity under stress, yet the molecular components governing this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify and characterize a septal pore-associated protein, SppA, and demonstrate its essential role in maintaining septal integrity in A. fumigatus. We show that expression of SppA is positively regulated by the transcription factor ZfpA and is induced in response to the cell wall-targeting antifungal caspofungin. Deletion of sppA resulted in defective septal organization and increased susceptibility to hyphal damage. The mutant exhibited heightened sensitivity to cell wall-targeting antifungal agents, indicating a role in cell wall stress tolerance. In a zebrafish model of invasive aspergillosis, loss of SppA significantly attenuated virulence which was abrogated in neutrophil-deficient zebrafish. Further, the mutant strain displayed increased susceptibility to killing by primary human neutrophils, suggesting that proper septal pore formation contributes to fungal survival during host immune attack. Together, our findings establish SppA as a critical determinant of septal integrity, antifungal tolerance, and pathogenicity in A. fumigatus, and position it as part of a ZfpA-regulated, caspofungin-responsive pathway that supports fungal survival during stress and infection. Author summary: Aspergillus fumigatus is a common environmental mold that can cause life-threatening infections in people with weakened immune systems. For successful invasion of host tissue, the fungus requires the ability to protection sections of its hyphae from cell wall targeting antifungals and host immune cell attack by closing septal (cross wall) pores distributed throughout hyphal strands. We have identified an A. fumigatus protein, SppA, required for proper septal pore closure. Loss of SppA reduces the ability of hyphae to withstand treatment with antifungals and the ability of A. fumigatus to cause disease in a zebrafish infection model. The SppA mutant was particularly susceptible to killing by neutrophils, key immune cells that help control fungal infections. Our findings reveal an important mechanism that helps A. fumigatus survive environmental and host-imposed stresses and highlight septal pore regulation as a potential target for future antifungal strategies.

candidates.title: Species diversity increases information flow about predation in bird communities
candidates.abstract: The Biodiversity-Ecosystem Functioning (BEF) literature has shown species diversity to be essential for ecosystem functioning and services. Yet this concept has not been extended often to behavioral ecology, so that although it is understood that acquiring social information from heterospecific individuals is an important component of ecosystem functioning, it is unclear how animal signaling at the community level, and subsequent information flow, is related to increased species diversity. Eliciting vocal responses using predator models across 10 nature reserves on a latitudinal gradient, we first show that the species diversity of birds is correlated with signaling about predation, both in the low-risk system of mobbing and in the higher-risk system of alarm calls. After finding a similar result across a fragment area gradient in one reserve, we used this system to test how interspecific information flow is affected by species diversity. Potential mechanisms behind this effect include that species are complementary in the characteristics of their mobbing calls, so more species translates into more cumulative information, or there are higher signaling rates as more individuals are involved, or a specific keystone species is more likely to occur. This experiment varied the number of species producing mobbing calls (one, two, four, eight species), with two playback construction methods (standardizing call rate, as typical for BEF experiments, or letting it increase with species richness, as in natural assemblages). Heterospecific mobbing participation (number of vocal species, number of participating individuals), and responses (call rate, probability to call in the first minute and frequency range) increased with species richness. Construction method significantly interacted with species richness, as non-standardized exemplars showed accentuated response as species richness increased. These results match expectations that complementary differences among species in the acoustic characteristics of mobbing calls, and increased call rate, both contribute to the result. There was little evidence that the signals of one particular species changed the experimental result. The overall evidence thus supports the hypothesis that the species diversity of a community is a key component influencing the quantity and the characteristics of signaling and information flow inside it. How information flows through animal communities and whether biodiversity enhances this process remain poorly understood. This study shows that greater bird species diversity increases predation-related signaling and information flow, highlighting a behavioral pathway linking biodiversity to ecosystem function.

candidates.title: Correction: Single-nucleus transcriptomics of wing sexual dimorphism and scale cell specialization in sulphur butterflies
candidates.abstract: by Ling S. Loh, Joseph J. Hanly, Alexander Carter, Martik Chatterjee, Martina Tsimba, Donya N. Shodja, Luca Livraghi, Christopher R. Day, Robert D. Reed, W. Owen McMillan, Gregory A. Wray, Arnaud Martin

candidates.title: Characterization and heterologous expression of surface polysaccharides from pathogenic Enterococcus cecorum .
candidates.abstract: Pathogenic variants of the chicken gastrointestinal bacterium Enterococcus cecorum are of growing concern due to their ability to cause vertebral osteomyelitis, such as enterococcal spondylitis or "kinky back," when the bacteria infect the free thoracic vertebrae of broilers. Due to the elimination of prophylactic antibiotic feed treatment that was previously used to manage the disease, there is now a need to develop other strategies for preventing pathogenic E. cecorum infections. In this work, we describe the structural characterization of two antigenic targets, a capsular polysaccharide and a rhamnopolysaccharide. Highly conserved biosynthetic gene clusters encoding enzymes for both structures have previously been identified in pathogenic E. cecorum . We show that these polysaccharides, when present on the surface of either the native or a heterologous host, induce an immune response in broilers. Furthermore, antibodies present in those sera cross-react with different E. cecorum strains and can induce killing of the pathogen in opsonophagocytosis assays. The characterization and heterologous expression of highly immunodominant cell wall polysaccharides that are conserved across many pathogenic strains is an important step toward the development of a potential glycoconjugate vaccine against E. cecorum .IMPORTANCE Enterococcus cecorum is a bacterium normally found in the gut of healthy chickens. However, pathogenic varieties of E. cecorum expressing surface capsular polysaccharides can cause skeletal deformations in the bird if the infection becomes systemic. This leads to severe morbidity and mortality in chickens raised for meat production and to significant financial losses for poultry producers. These infections were once managed by the inclusion of antibiotics in chicken feed; but this practice has been discontinued due to concern over antibiotic resistance development. We have identified polysaccharides that are conserved on the surface of many pathogenic E. cecorum that induce protective cross-reactive immune responses in chickens when the polysaccharides are expressed on a benign bacterial carrier. As an alternative to antibiotics, this is an important first step toward the development of a vaccine that specifically targets many pathogenic E. cecorum isolates and may help to reduce financial losses while improving animal welfare.

candidates.title: KvrA promotes pulmonary persistence and systemic dissemination of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae .
candidates.abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp) poses a severe threat to human health, with KvrA, a member of the SlyA family of MarR-type transcriptional regulators, previously shown to contribute to capsule production, hypermucoviscosity formation, and virulence in Klebsiella pneumoniae . However, whether KvrA coordinates additional surface-associated pathways during infection remains incompletely understood. This study systematically investigated the role of KvrA in the survival, dissemination, and colonization of hvKp through in vitro and in vivo experiments. We found that knocking out kvrA in K. pneumoniae KPPR1 resulted in a capsular-deficient phenotype in bacterial colonies. KvrA was confirmed to positively regulate the expression of capsular polysaccharide (CPS)-associated genes, thereby promoting the synthesis of CPS. The Δ kvrA mutant displayed reduced survival rate when exposed to human serum, and the amount of its biofilm formation also decreased. Furthermore, in vitro , macrophages significantly phagocytosed more Δ kvrA mutant than wild type, indicating that KvrA contributes to phagocytic resistance of hvKp. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that KvrA regulates additional surface-associated pathways, including lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis and type 3 fimbria-associated biofilm formation. A murine pneumonia infection model revealed that the Δ kvrA mutant exhibited higher bacterial clearance in the lung, liver, and spleen compared with the wild-type strain, indicating that KvrA contributes to in vivo survival, dissemination, and colonization of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp). Histopathological observations further corroborated the contribution of KvrA to hvKp pathogenicity in mice. Collectively, our findings extend previous studies by demonstrating that KvrA not only regulates capsule-associated virulence traits but also coordinates additional surface-associated pathways, including LPS biosynthesis and type 3 fimbria/biofilm-related processes, contributing to pulmonary persistence and systemic dissemination of hvKp.IMPORTANCE Klebsiella pneumoniae is an opportunistic pathogen that has emerged as a significant causative agent for both community-acquired and nosocomial infections. The emergence of highly virulent and multidrug-resistant strains of K. pneumoniae poses a substantial threat to public health. The gene kvrA plays a pivotal role in the colonization and pathogenicity of K. pneumoniae . Understanding the regulatory mechanisms of KvrA in K. pneumoniae provides a theoretical basis for identifying novel genetic targets to control K. pneumoniae infections, which may facilitate the development of therapeutic agents.

candidates.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
candidates.abstract: by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

candidates.title: Crop diversification promotes soil microbial carbon turnover.
candidates.abstract: Agricultural diversification alters plant residue chemistry and rhizodeposition, with legacy effects on soil organic matter (SOM) cycling. The priming effect (PE) and necromass formation are key processes of SOM dynamics, yet how diversification affects these processes, and SOM persistence remains poorly understood. Using 13C-labelled glucose in a 150-day incubation of soils (0-15 cm) from two contrasting diversification trials (43 and 8 years), we found that diversification increased SOM priming by 153-174% and retention of glucose-derived 13C in microbial necromass by 227-289%. Diversified soils also had more bioavailable C, dissolved organic C, and neutral sugars, stronger stoichiometric nutrient limitation (103% higher C:P imbalance and 15% lower vector angle), and higher microbial activity and N- and P-acquiring enzyme activities. Microbial C use efficiency increased by 65%, while replacing the native microbial community of diversified soils with that of conventional soils reduced CUE by 9% and 45% at the 43- and 8-year sites, respectively. Community-level analyses further linked greater retention of glucose-derived 13C in microbial necromass to putative Discosea and Bacillota co-occurrence patterns. Metagenomic profiling revealed 18-125% higher relative abundances of CAZyme genes involved in degrading plant- and microbial-derived compounds, alongside a modest (~4%) increase in Y-associated functional potential at both sites. Although priming-induced native-C losses exceeded the amount of glucose-derived 13C retained in microbial necromass, the ratio of necromass C retention to priming-induced C loss was 28% higher under diversification than under conventional cropping over the 150-day incubation. Crop diversification thus reshapes microbial C cycling, coupling enhanced native SOM mineralization with greater retention of added C in microbial necromass, making the net effect on SOC dependent on sustained C inputs.

candidates.title: Environmental microbial exposure as an under-measured exposome domain: Links to host microbiomes, immune regulation, and disease epidemiology.
candidates.abstract: Environmental microbial exposure is an under-measured biological component of the exposome and a plausible determinant of immune-mediated disease patterns. Humans encounter microbial communities and products from soil, air, water, vegetation, animals, food systems, farms, indoor dust, healthcare settings, schools, and urban built environments. These exposures may influence gut, skin, airway, oral, and mucosal microbiomes and thereby alter epithelial barrier function, immune tolerance, inflammatory thresholds, and microbial metabolite production. This structured mechanistic narrative review integrates direct environmental-exposure studies, environment-to-host microbiome studies, host-microbiome mechanistic evidence, and translational frameworks. The clearest convergence occurs in asthma and allergic disease, where early-life farm exposure, endotoxin-rich dust, environmental microbial diversity, innate immune modulation, and epithelial A20 regulation support a coherent exposure-response model. Evidence for inflammatory bowel disease and broader respiratory outcomes is biologically credible but less direct, whereas metabolic and systemic inflammatory outcomes remain largely supported by host-microbiome and metabolite mechanisms rather than direct environmental exposure studies. The review therefore distinguishes evidence maturity and mechanistic proximity rather than treating all disease categories equally. It further positions pollution, urbanization, building design, biodiversity loss, diet, antibiotics, and socioeconomic conditions as active modifiers of microbial exposure and host response. Future studies should integrate direct environmental sampling with body-site microbiome profiling, functional multi-omics, immune and barrier biomarkers, geospatial exposure assessment, source tracking, repeated measures, and explicit causal-inference designs. Environmental microbial exposure should be treated neither as uniformly beneficial nor harmful, but as a measurable, context-dependent exposome domain whose health effects depend on composition, dose, timing, route, co-exposures, and host susceptibility.
candidates.journal: Journal of environmental health science & engineering

candidates.title: Single-molecule whole-genome sequencing reveals genomic and epigenomic concordance between ultrasonic aspiration and surgical resection in meningioma: prospective feasibility series.
candidates.abstract: Background Ultrasonic surgical aspirators, including Sonopet ® , are widely used during skull base meningioma resection to enable safe tumor debulking in constrained corridors, but aspirated tumor fragments are often discarded. Whether this tissue supports genomic and epigenomic profiling comparable to standard resection tissue is unknown. The aim of this study was to determine whether Sonopet ® aspirate is a viable substrate for long-read genomic and epigenomic profiling in skull base meningioma. Methods We prospectively collected paired standard resection (R) and Sonopet ® aspirate (S) specimens from seven patients with skull base meningioma and performed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read whole-genome sequencing using PromethION R10 flow cells. We compared sequencing yield, read quality, tumor purity, copy-number profiles, somatic single-nucleotide variant (SNV) burden, variant allele frequency, and CpG methylation between matched samples, then projected methylation profiles onto a reference framework of 121 EPIC array-profiled samples for molecular group classification. Results Aspirates generated sequencing yields, read lengths, and tumor purity comparable to matched specimens. Copy-number profiles were largely concordant and recovered canonical meningioma alterations, with close agreement in total and loss burden (Lin's CCC = 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.00). SNV burden showed moderate agreement (CCC = 0.53, 95% CI - 0.28 to 0.99), with two discordant patients possibly reflecting intratumoral heterogeneity. Promoter methylation was closely correlated between pairs (Pearson r > 0.99 across ~ 177,000 promoters), and molecular group classification was concordant in all pairs except P1, where tumor purity was uncertain. Conclusions Sonopet ® aspirate provides tissue comparable to standard resection specimens for long-read genomic and epigenomic profiling, supporting its use as a substrate for molecular diagnosis and translational research, particularly for subtotally resected tumors with limited tissue.

candidates.title: Mitochondrial Phylogeny Reveals Deep Intraspecific Divergence and Fine-Scale Regional Structure in Orangutans.
candidates.abstract: Orangutans ( Pongo spp.) are a valuable model for investigating how past climatic and geological events have shaped population structure and species diversification. We reconstructed 237 complete mitochondrial genomes from whole-genome sequencing data and combined them with 50 available mitochondrial sequences, resulting in a dataset of 287 orangutans spanning the current range of Sumatran and Bornean orangutans. Among Sumatran orangutans ( P. abelii ), we identified five geographically distinct mitochondrial clades corresponding to Langkat, North Aceh, Tripa, West Leuser and Batu Ardan. These clades showed strong differentiation, indicating long-term persistence of distinct maternal lineages across the Leuser landscape. For the recently described species, P. tapanuliensis , we added 10 newly reconstructed mitogenomes, increasing representation from 3 to 13 individuals. P. tapanuliensis formed a monophyletic, deeply divergent clade, confirming strong mitochondrial differentiation and long-term isolation. In Bornean orangutans ( P. pygmaeus ), we identified seven major regional mitochondrial clades corresponding to Sarawak, Central Kalimantan, South Kalimantan, Southeast Kalimantan, East Kalimantan and the North and South Kinabatangan populations in Sabah. Within the subspecies P. p. morio , the North and South Kinabatangan, East Kalimantan and Southeast Kalimantan clades formed distinct maternal lineages, revealing substantial mitochondrial structure within the currently recognised subspecies. Our findings suggest that current geographic and taxonomic divisions may under-represent the extent of regional maternal diversity across orangutans. Female philopatry has preserved ancient mitochondrial structure across Sundaland, with its geographic distribution shaped by refugial persistence, major riverine barriers and long-term population fragmentation.

candidates.title: Inbreeding in the genomics era: comparing IBD, drift, and homozygosity-based methods in a pig breeding population.
candidates.abstract: Background The inbreeding and kinship methods can be classified into three approaches: (1) Identity-by-Descent (IBD) estimates the probability that alleles are identical by shared ancestry; (2) Drift-based methods measure deviations in allele frequencies from a base due to genetic drift; and (3) Homozygosity-based (HOM) methods estimate genome-wide homozygosity. The objective of this study was to compare the estimated inbreeding and kinship rates using those three approaches. Within each approach, different methods were investigated. The dataset consisted of purebred sires from artificial insemination centers born between 2014 and 2024, along with their relatives with genotype data, totaling 152,883 pigs. Animals were genotyped with various SNP panels and imputed to medium- and high-density panels (50 K and 660 K). Results For inbreeding estimates, correlations among IBD-based methods were high (0.88), while correlations among drift-based methods ranged from 0.74 to 0.91. Homozygosity-based estimates showed a wide range of correlations (- 0.03 to 1.00). This variability was mainly driven by low or negative correlations involving short runs of homozygosity (ROH) classes (2-4 Mb and 4-8 Mb), which showed poor agreement with longer ROH categories. Correlations between methods from different approaches were generally weak to high (- 0.09 to 0.81). Kinship estimates showed higher correlations than inbreeding estimates. Nevertheless, the same pattern was observed: correlations were consistently higher within the same approach (above 0.96) than across different approaches (above 0.70). Rates of inbreeding and kinship per generation, estimated as regression slopes across birth years and converted to a per-generation scale, were consistently higher for drift-based measures than for the other approaches. This indicates that drift-based and homozygosity-based measures are not equivalent under genomic selection. Their differences are proportional to the covariance between changes in allele frequency and initial allele frequencies. Consequently, minor alleles tend to increase in frequency more often than expected under neutrality in this pig breeding line. Conclusions Overall, the results show that different approaches to estimating inbreeding and kinship convey distinct biological information. Homozygosity-based measures yielded lower estimates than drift-based metrics, suggesting non-neutral dynamics of allele frequencies. These findings indicate that constraining inbreeding using a drift-based genomic relationship matrix within an optimum contribution selection scheme may improve the management of genetic diversity.

candidates.title: Gray bats heighten their response to social cues when navigating group flight in environments with obstacles.
candidates.abstract: Bats are fast fliers with great maneuverability. Many species sense and communicate through echolocation, relying on acoustic signals in the environment. Bats also form large colonies, which necessitates that they fly in groups. When group size increases or obstacles are in their flight paths, the acoustic space can become cluttered, posing a non-trivial challenge for navigation. How do they interact with their environment and conspecifics, and how do they balance social and environmental cues? Recent research has uncovered individual adaptations to calling and flight patterns when flying in the groups or avoiding obstacles. Studies also suggest coordination when foraging, as well as strategies used by the group to mitigate acoustic clutter. However, there has yet to be a study on how bats weigh different navigational tasks when flying in spatially complex environments. Here, we collected stereoscopic video data from a wild colony of gray bats, Myotis grisescens, navigating their usual foraging flight paths in the presence of novel obstacles. We find that bats tend to stay close to a wall, but space out when flying in groups. We develop a data-informed agent-based model which reveals that their social repulsive behavior is strengthened when challenged to navigate novel obstacles.

candidates.title: Explainable machine learning-assisted exploration of chromatin dynamics reveals chromosome-specific response to serum starvation.
candidates.abstract: Chromatin is dynamic at all length scales, influencing chromatin-based processes, such as gene expression. Even large-scale reorganization of whole chromosome territories has been reported upon specific signals, but the lack of suitable methods has prevented analysis of the underlying dynamic processes. Here, we have used CRISPR-Sirius for time-lapse imaging of chromatin loci dynamics during serum starvation. We show that chromosome 1 loci move toward the nuclear envelope during the first hour of serum starvation in a chromosome-specific manner. Machine learning-assisted exploration of acquired multiparametric data combined with the Shapley values-based explanation approach allowed us to uncover the critical features that characterize chromatin dynamics during serum starvation. This analysis reveals that although serum starvation affects overall nuclear morphology and chromatin dynamics, chromosome 1 loci display a specific response that is characterized by maintenance of dynamics in a constrained environment, and long 'jumps' at the nuclear periphery. Interestingly, the two homologous chromosomes display differential behaviors, with the more peripheral homolog being more responsive to the signal than the internal one. Overall, the presented machine learning-assisted dataset exploration helps us navigate the multidimensional data to understand the underlying dynamic processes and can be applied to a wide variety of research questions in imaging and cell biology in general.

candidates.title: Rethinking laboratory sustainability.
candidates.abstract: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. I argue that a more meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must look beyond physical resource management to examine the scientific process itself; to rethink the questions we ask, the experiments we do, and how we communicate our findings. To build a truly sustainable scientific ecosystem, Green Lab initiatives must join forces with Open Science and research integrity movements to update not only the hardware, but also the software of science.

candidates.title: Junctional and actomyosin dynamics drive endothelial cell rearrangements during vascular tube formation.
candidates.abstract: Lumen formation is a key process during the morphogenesis of tubular organs, such as the vertebrate vascular network. At the cellular level, lumen formation can be achieved by cell shape changes or cell rearrangements. We have previously shown that such cell rearrangements are driven by oscillating membrane protrusions, called junction-based lamellipodia (JBL), which provide a ratchet mechanism driving convergent cell movements to connect local lumens, and generate vascular patency. By performing in vivo time-lapse imaging at high spatiotemporal resolution in zebrafish embryos, we have analyzed the cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics, which underlie JBL formation and function. We show that JBL formation requires the activity of the F-actin nucleation complex Arp2/3. We further show that a novel junction is formed at the distal end of the JBL from a pool of VE-cadherin originating from outside the initial JBL area. Subsequently, proximal and distal junctions merge and fuse, a process driven by actomyosin contractility. Prior to this fusion, we observe a specific recruitment of Myl9 within the interjunctional space. Furthermore, inhibition of actomyosin contractility abrogates junctional merging. Taken together, our analyses demonstrate that JBL constitute a module, which, by alternate generation of pushing forces (JBL formation) and pulling forces (junctional merging), provide the physical means for endothelial cells to elongate and to rearrange and thereby generate a continuous vascular lumen.

candidates.title: Diurnal rhythmicity in metabolism and salivary effector expression shapes aphid performance on host plants.
candidates.abstract: Diurnal rhythms influence insect behavior, physiology, and metabolism, optimizing their performance by adapting to daily changes in the environment. While their impact on agricultural pests has been briefly explored, our understanding of how these rhythms drive adaptive responses in pest biology and influence host colonization remains elusive. Here, we show that a notorious global aphid pest, Rhopalosiphum padi , exhibits distinct diurnal patterns in feeding behavior, with elevated honeydew excretion at night and extended phloem salivation during early nighttime. Temporal aphid transcriptome profiling reveals four diurnally rhythmic clusters, two of which peak at night, exhibiting enrichment in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. Beyond the established role in manipulating host responses and allowing sustained feeding, our study reveals novel evidence of cyclical fluctuations in salivary effector expression in an insect species. Silencing key effector genes, peaking in expression during the increased nighttime salivation, results in a more pronounced reduction in aphid excretion activity on host plants during the night compared to the day, a phenomenon not observed on artificial diets. A better understanding of aphid diurnal rhythms and their roles in shaping aphid performance provides a promising avenue to refine and optimize pest management, granting a strategic advantage for minimizing crop damage.

candidates.title: Adaptive sampling: information-guided selection for targeted long-read sequencing and epigenetic studies.
candidates.abstract: Adaptive sampling (AS) is a unique feature of nanopore sequencing that enables real-time enrichment or depletion of target molecules during the sequencing run based on their initial sequence information. AS provides a flexible and scalable alternative to conventional capture- and amplification-based approaches, while preserving long reads and the ability to detect epigenetic modifications of native DNA/RNA molecules. In this review, we summarize the principles of AS-based sequencing, explain the enrichment- and depletion-mode strategies and discuss factors affecting its performance. We further highlight the growing body of studies demonstrating the utility of AS across a diverse range of applications, such as metagenomic and microbiome research, structural variant characterization and discovery, studying repeat expansion disorders, integrated genetic and epigenetic profiling or transcriptome analysis. In these and other contexts, AS enables efficient allocation of sequencing capacity toward biologically relevant molecules, while accelerating data generation, which also makes it applicable to rapid molecular diagnostics and real-time genomic analyses in clinical practice. As nanopore sequencing continues to mature and become a standard analysis approach in many laboratories, AS is likely to evolve from a specialized enrichment strategy into a routine component of genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic workflows.

candidates.title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
candidates.abstract: by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans . The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

candidates.title: Local feedback governs cell fate transition to drive self-organized phenotypic equilibrium in hierarchical tumors
candidates.abstract: by Emma Legait, Charlotte Rulquin, Lauranne Bouteille, Raphaël Clément, Cédric Maurange How cell-state transitions are regulated along a tumor lineage to determine its overall cellular composition remains unclear. Using a simple hierarchical tumor model in Drosophila , we show that differentiation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) into transit amplifying progenitors (TAPs) depends on the fraction of TAPs among their immediate neighbors. This relationship is captured by a local feedback transition rule that quantitatively predicts CSC transition probability. Implementing this rule in 3D growth simulations spontaneously recapitulates CSC clustering and the emergence of a stable CSC fraction within tumors. Mechanistically, the local feedback is mediated by EGFR signaling from newly produced TAPs, propagating differentiation across CSC clusters. Consistently, we show that clustering protects the CSC pool from depletion driven by surrounding TAPs, indicating that spatial architecture and lineage dynamics are tightly coupled. Together, these findings show that a local feedback governing fate transitions drives emergent spatial organization that stabilizes the stem cell fraction in hierarchical tumors.

candidates.title: Migration as a key influence on ungulate eco-evolutionary history
candidates.abstract: by Gustavo Burin Species can overcome resource limitations by migrating to more favourable areas. A new study in PLOS Biology shows that migration has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, that likely led to changes in ecosystem functioning. Species can overcome environmental limitations by migrating to more favorable areas. This Primer explores a new study in PLOS Biology showing that this behavior has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, which in turn likely led to changes in ecosystem properties and functioning.

candidates.title: An indirect wing steering muscle stabilizes flight by regulating wing pitch angle in Drosophila
candidates.abstract: by Han Kheng Teoh, Debojyoti Biswas, Haoru Li, Abby Leung, B. Kemper Ludlow, Samuel C. Whitehead, Erica Ehrhardt, Michael Dickinson, Tsevi Beatus, Noah J. Cowan, Itai Cohen Flapping flight is inherently unstable, requiring Drosophila to fine-tune their wing motions on a milliseconds timescale. Pioneering studies have shown that the direct steering muscles, which attach to the wing hinge, are important for generating these rapid flight reflexes. Recent connectome data, however, reveal that indirect steering muscles or tension muscles, which alter the mechanics of the thorax, receive some of the same synaptic inputs from the sensory apparatus as the direct steering muscles. This discovery suggests that the indirect steering muscles may also be important for flight control. Here, we show that the indirect tergopleural muscles indeed contribute substantially to stabilization, particularly for large pitch perturbations. We find that for small perturbations (less than 1,000 °/s), flies modulate their wing stroke amplitude to generate lift-based corrective torques, a strategy that has been previously documented. For larger perturbations, however, we observe that Drosophila engage an additional wing degree of freedom—the wing pitch angle—to leverage additional lift and drag forces during the corrective maneuver. Quasi-steady aerodynamic simulations reveal that this strategy minimizes power consumption, anaolgous to how some mammals (including humans) adjust their steady-state gaits in a near energy-optimal manner. Using optogenetics and a control theory framework, we demonstrate that the tergopleural muscle is activated by a proportional gain component of a nonlinear proportional-integral controller responsible for determining the wing pitch angle during large perturbations. A simplified torsional spring model for the wing hinge captures the changes in the wing pitch dynamics observed during correction maneuvers by using the tergopleural muscle to adjust the rest angle of the wing. These findings provide a striking example of reflex strategy selection in time-critical behaviors and underscore the vital role of indirect steering muscles in flight stabilization.

candidates.title: Long-lasting chromatin and transcriptional states shape the maintenance of memory ensembles
candidates.abstract: Memories of recent events are stored within minutes in neuronal ensembles in the hippocampus. Over days to weeks, these memories undergo consolidation, and later retrieval depends on reactivation of a subset of neurons within the ensemble. However, how transient experiences produce lasting molecular and cellular changes in hippocampal ensemble neurons remains unknown. Here, we profile the functional, transcriptional, and gene regulatory states of hippocampal memory ensemble neurons at single cell resolution across multiple remote timepoints following single trial contextual fear conditioning. We uncover long lasting, cell type specific chromatin and gene expression changes after learning that coincide with sustained shifts in synaptic plasticity. Within dentate gyrus granule ensembles, we identify a persistent chromatin transcriptional program that emerges in a subset of ensemble neurons and is marked by sustained expression of many synaptic genes. This transcriptional signature predicts which neurons will be reactivated during memory recall, suggesting that only a fraction of initial ensemble neurons maintains a molecular state supporting later reactivation. Regulatory elements associated with this persistent state are highly enriched for AP1 motifs, the cognate binding sites for Fos family transcription factors, even though FOS protein has long since decayed away. Instead, we detect long lasting FOSB binding at these elements, suggesting a mechanism by which the effects of immediate early gene driven transcription are extended beyond the initial induction window. FOSB is particularly enriched in ensemble neurons that maintain enduring gene expression changes, suggesting it sustains chromatin accessibility and prolonged transcription in neurons reactivatable during memory retrieval. Together, these findings identify molecular mechanisms underlying the maintenance, maturation, and evolution of hippocampal memory ensembles over time.

candidates.title: Transcriptomic and Lipidomic Profiling of Human iPSC-Derived Microglia Reveals TREM2-Dependent and -Independent Processes
candidates.abstract: TREM2 has been implicated in AD as a critical regulator of microglial functions and loss of function mutations in TREM2 increases one's risk of developing AD. Given the diverse functional roles of TREM2, we sought to unravel how it affects downstream pathways using human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) derived from TREM2 knockout (KO) and isogenic control lines and assessing the response to oligomeric amyloid-{beta} 42 (oA{beta}42). While previous studies have primarily used fibrillar A{beta}, we focused on microglial responses to oA{beta}42 given their disease relevance and potent cytotoxic effects. At baseline, we identified a set of TREM2-dependent genes, which corresponded to the DAM signature in mice and disease-associated signatures in humans. Additionally, loss of TREM2 resulted in increased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. In response to oA{beta}42, we found that the transcriptional response was largely TREM2-independent and corresponded to a strong induction of inflammatory pathways, with TREM2 also being downregulated in control iMGLs. We identified subsets of genes and pathways that were unique to either control, such as mitochondrial DNA and RNA degradation, or TREM2 KO iMGLs, such as the senescence-associated secretory pathway and adipogenesis, suggesting some differences in gene expression driven by TREM2 in response to oA{beta}42. Given that the inflammatory response was TREM2-independent, we sought to identify signaling pathways that contributed to inflammation. Inhibition of toll-like receptor signaling significantly reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes and modestly increased expression of TREM2 and TREM2-dependent genes. Consistent with our transcriptional data, cytokine production and secretion in response to oA{beta}42 was significantly increased to similar levels in both controls and TREM2 KO iMGLs. Lipidomic profiling of microglia revealed that triglycerides and lactosylceramides were significantly increased in both control and TREM2 KO iMGLs in response to oA{beta}42. TREM2 KO iMGLs had decreased levels of BMPs and increased levels of cholesterol esters across all conditions, further highlighting a role for TREM2 in maintaining lipid homeostasis in microglia. Taken together, we describe genes, pathways, and lipids that are associated with TREM2 expression that likely influence microglial responses to oA{beta}42.

candidates.title: In vivo crosslinking and cryo-EM analyses suggest a revised model of conjugative pilus biogenesis
candidates.abstract: Bacterial conjugation requires elaboration of a conjugative pilus by membrane-embedded transport machineries known as Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SSs). Recent structural findings suggested a model of conjugative pilus biogenesis in which the pilus is assembled from the VirB6-base of the T4SS Stalk, while the VirB5-apex is projected at the pilus tip. In this study, we show that in vivo crosslinking of these two Stalk segments within the R388 T4SS has only a modest effect on conjugative transfer efficiency, inconsistent with them separating during pilus elaboration. Combined with cryo-electron microscopy analyses of the homologous pKM101 T4SS, this leads us to propose a revised model, in which the sixfold-symmetrical inner membrane complex of the T4SS serves directly as a base for assembly of the fivefold-symmetrical pilus. The resulting symmetry mismatch is resolved by the sequential incorporation of pilus subunits at a continuously repositioning gap at the base of the nascent pilus. This revised model answers the long-standing question of how T4SSs accommodate a central symmetry mismatch during a crucial process of bacterial conjugation underpinning horizontal gene transfer.

candidates.title: In the non-canonical NF-κB pathway, binding of the initiating kinase NIK to the pathway's target, p100, serves a nonenzymatic "licensing" role
candidates.abstract: The non-canonical NF-{kappa}B pathway plays pivotal roles in adaptive immunity. It is initiated by NIK-mediated phosphorylation of IKK1, which phosphorylates p100 and promotes processing of newly synthesized p100. However, IKK1 can also be activated by other kinases to mediate distinct functions. Why IKK1-induced p100 processing occurs efficiently downstream of NIK but not of other kinases is unknown. Here, we show that whereas pre-existing p100 can be phosphorylated by IKK1 without NIK, phosphorylation of newly synthesized p100 critically depends on additional non-enzymatic functions of NIK's C-terminal portion. NIK binds IKK1 and restrains its kinase activity, while its binding to p100 enhances p100 phosphorylation. Single-molecule FRET spectroscopy and XL-MS revealed that the C-terminal region of p100 adopts a folded-back conformation and undergoes structural rearrangement upon NIK binding, likely accounting for this enhancement. Thus, NIK not only initiates the pathway but also dictates its specificity through binding to its downstream substrate.

candidates.title: Development of synthetic genetic arrays for studying interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes
candidates.abstract: Mitochondria, the central axis of metabolism and energy transformation has emerged as a focal point for understanding the aging process and a plethora of human diseases. Yet, how the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes communicate is still unclear. This work aims to allow the analysis of such crosstalk by developing a genome-wide platform for studying genetic interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Using yeast as a model system in which mitochondrial homoplasmy and stable alterations in the mitochondrial genome can be generated by biolistic bombardment, we created a genome-wide library of yeast cells carrying nuclear deletions and temperature-sensitive mutations together with a superfolder-GFP reporter for the expression of the mitochondrial-encoded COX2 gene. Using this approach, we found links between nuclear-encoded processes and mitochondrial gene expression not previously anticipated, including a requirement for genes involved in MVB (multivesicular body) sorting/RIM signaling, vesicle trafficking/glycosylation, polarity, and peroxisome biogenesis, for maintaining mitochondrial COX2 expression. In contrast, defects in the autophagy machineries, ribosome biogenesis, and nuclear transcription and chromatin organization resulted in increased expression of COX2. While reduced COX2 expression correlated with a reduced expression of the nuclear-encoded TOM70 gene in mutants defect in mitochondrial functions, expression of the mitochondrial and nuclear genes responded differently to defects in cytoplasmic ribosome biogenesis and autophagy. When creating the COX2 expression library, we also found that cells devoid of mitochondrial DNA rely on the Rim101 signaling pathway, and many of its auxiliary regulatory factors, to maintain fitness. As mutations in the Rim101 signaling pathway also caused down-regulation of COX2 expression, it appears that Rim101 signaling is central for maintaining proper control of mitochondrial function. We believe the approach will allow for future genome-wide studies on how nuclear-encoded processes influence the translation, protein folding, and processing of mitochondria-encoded genes.

candidates.title: Single-molecule tracking in the psychrophile Psychrobacter cryohalolentis reveals heat-shock-induced changes in ClpX dynamics
candidates.abstract: Psychrophilic organisms display a series of physiological adaptations which enable them to thrive in cold environments, yet the dynamics of these processes in living cells remain largely unexplored. Here, we establish super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule tracking (SMT) in the cold-adapted bacterium Psychrobacter cryohalolentis, enabling the investigation of protein dynamics in vivo at high spatiotemporal resolution. For controlled expression of HaloTag fusions in this organism, we developed an inducible plasmid expression system based on a galactose-inducible promoter. As a proof of concept, we followed the AAA+ unfoldase ClpX during steady-state growth and heat shock. At 22 {degrees}C, ClpX diffused as a single population with a media apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.25 m2/s, suggesting that most molecules reside in large complexes. A shift to 32 {degrees}C, above the growth maximum of this strain, broadened the mobility distribution, increasing both slow and fast populations, and transiently redistributed ClpX towards the cell periphery. During recovery the fast population returned to baseline within 5 min, whereas the slow population remained elevated for at least 30 min, suggesting that the two populations reflect distinct processes. SMT in a psychrophilic bacterium thus opens new possibilities to study how cold-adapted microorganisms respond to environmental change at the molecular level.

candidates.title: Sidetrak: a de novo-designed miniprotein targets the kinesin-1 coiled-coil stalk to inhibit MAP7 binding and disrupt mitochondrial transport
candidates.abstract: The coiled-coil domains of cytoskeletal motors contain regulatory surfaces that offer largely unexploited targets for manipulating intracellular transport. The microtubule-associated protein MAP7 promotes kinesin-1 motor activity, binding a coiled-coil surface that overlaps the TPR docking site (TDS), a regulatory interface involved in autoinhibition. Starting from an AlphaFold3 model of this relatively feature-poor surface, we used BoltzGen to design Sidetrak, a 36-amino acid miniprotein that binds kinesin-1 with nanomolar affinity. Binding requires the TDS and is abolished by mutation of the predicted Sidetrak interface, supporting the modelled local geometry of the targeted coiled-coil region. Sidetrak inhibits MAP7 binding, reduces MAP7-dependent kinesin-1 recruitment to microtubules in cells and causes perinuclear redistribution of mitochondria, a kinesin-1 cargo. Sidetrak binds all three kinesin-1 heavy-chain paralogues, and quantitative interaction proteomics revealed selective association with endogenous kinesin-1 complexes and associated cargo adaptors. These findings demonstrate selective disruption of a motor-MAP interaction by a de novo-designed protein and highlight regulatory coiled-coil surfaces as targets for manipulating intracellular transport. Beyond providing a means to manipulate intracellular transport, this work illustrates the potential of de novo protein design to test structural models of protein interfaces and probe endogenous protein networks to uncover underlying cellular mechanisms.

candidates.title: Repeated regeneration prolongs the juvenile stage and extends lifespan in the annelid Platynereis dumerilii
candidates.abstract: Regeneration restores tissues lost to injury, but its consequences may extend beyond local repair. Whether regeneration produces lasting systemic effects on developmental timing and lifespan remains poorly understood. Here we investigated the long-term consequences of repeated regeneration in the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii. To determine these consequences, we repeatedly amputated juveniles at monthly intervals, removing approximately half of the body after each regenerative cycle, and compared them with control unamputated siblings. Repeatedly regenerating worms lived approximately 1.5-fold longer than controls and showed delayed sexual maturation, including delayed gametogenic progression at the morphological and transcriptional levels. Somatic progression was also delayed, as indicated by slower accumulation of pigmentation associated with developmental progression, while regenerative competence was maintained across amputations. To investigate whether regeneration engages distant tissues, we compared head transcriptomes from amputated and unamputated worms. Posterior amputation altered head gene expression within 2 hours, including increased expression of genes associated with younger head profiles, such as igf-like and alpha-tubulin. Together, our results show that repeated regeneration not only restores lost tissues but prolongs the juvenile state, delays reproductive and somatic maturation, and extends lifespan, a phenomenon we term the Highlander effect. These findings suggest that regeneration may influence organismal life history beyond tissue replacement, with neurohormonal signaling as a potential mediator.

candidates.title: A unifying framework for structured population dynamics in modern coexistence theory
candidates.abstract: Variation within populations is ubiquitous in nature, yet many models and frameworks in community ecology assume that all individuals within a population interact with the community identically. Modern coexistence theory is no exception; however, several subfields of ecology have independently been integrating coexistence theory, each asking the same underlying question: how do structured population dynamics shape coexistence outcomes? Here, I propose a unifying framework for integrating population variation into modern coexistence theory that is applicable across all fields of ecology. The application of this framework is presented in three case studies: niche overlap and fitness differences between influenza substrains, mutual invasibility between competing perennial plants, and fluctuation-dependent invasion outcomes in apparently competing prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff. Together, these examples illustrate the framework's broad applicability, power to resolve the interaction between population and community level processes, and its potential to reveal novel ecological phenomena.

candidates.title: Microeukaryotic indicators of freshwater ecosystem condition from a national river monitoring network
candidates.abstract: Microeukaryotes are a diverse and functionally important component of river biofilms, including primary producers, consumers, decomposers, and parasites and symbionts. However, their diversity is likely underestimated, and their composition, environmental drivers, and seasonal dynamics have rarely been studied at large spatial scales. Microbiological monitoring of freshwater ecosystems has historically focused almost entirely on diatoms, so the potential of the wider microbial community as indicators of river condition is unknown. Here, we used 18S rRNA gene metabarcoding of more than 1,600 biofilm samples from 700 sites across England's River Surveillance Network. We show that communities were dominated by diatoms, chlorophytes, ciliates, and fungi, and shifted from phototroph-dominated biofilms in spring towards more diverse, heterotroph-rich biofilms in autumn. Community turnover was driven by water chemistry rather than geographic distance, with alkalinity, DO, temperature, and nitrate-N among the strongest drivers of composition. Co-occurrence networks resolved assemblages of taxa with shared environmental responses, and threshold indicator taxa analysis identified ASV-level indicators of water chemistry gradients. Community change points along these gradients closely matched those reported for bacteria from the same biofilms, and several taxa declined at lower concentrations than the community as a whole, offering potential early warning of change. These findings show that the microeukaryotic community tracks water chemistry consistently across a national river network and can provide a taxonomically broad set of sensitive and interpretable indicators of river condition that complement diatom-based monitoring and emerging bacterial approaches.

candidates.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation for pediatric Clostridioides difficile infection: efficacy, challenges, and the path to next-generation microbiome therapies.
candidates.abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is an increasing cause of morbidity in children, with recurrent disease posing substantial therapeutic challenges. Antibiotic therapy remains the cornerstone of initial management; however, up to 30% of children experience recurrence, and those with underlying comorbidities face recurrence rates as high as 65%.
