Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has demonstrated superior efficacy over antibiotics for recurrent CDI (rCDI) in adults and has emerged as the most effective available intervention for pediatric rCDI. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on FMT efficacy, microbiome changes, and safety in children with CDI. Data from large multicenter cohort studies demonstrate cure rates exceeding 80%, with comparable efficacy observed in high-risk subpopulations, including those with inflammatory bowel disease and immunocompromising conditions. Critical research gaps remain, including the absence of randomized controlled trials and limited long-term safety data in children. Despite demonstrated effectiveness, significant barriers limit FMT accessibility for children. The COVID-19 pandemic has substantially impacted availability, and current regulatory changes have further restricted access. The lack of FDA-approved live biotherapeutic products approved for CDI in children creates additional challenges. We critically examine the emerging pipeline of next-generation microbiome-based therapies and identify the steps required to ensure children with recurrent CDI have access to safe, effective, and approved treatments.

[Background]
Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is one of the leading healthcare-associated infections, with incidence rising over recent decades in both adults and children and an increasing shift toward community acquisition. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has transformed the management of recurrent CDI (rCDI) in adults and demonstrated superiority over standard antibiotic therapy in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). 1 , 2 These compelling outcomes have prompted exploration of FMT in children with rCDI, where up to 30% of patients fail standard antibiotic therapy, and those with underlying conditions face recurrence rates as high as 65%. 3 Large observational studies have demonstrated FMT cure rates exceeding 80% in pediatric rCDI. However, recent restrictions on FMT access and the absence of approved microbiome-based live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) for patients under 18 have created a significant unmet need in children with recurrent and refractory disease. In this review, we discuss the rationale and efficacy of FMT for CDI in children, and critically examine the challenges – regulatory, biological, and therapeutic – that must be overcome to translate these findings into accessible, approved treatments for pediatric patients (Graphical abstract). This narrative review was conducted through a systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through April 2026. The search terms included combinations of: “Clostridioides difficile,” “Clostridium difficile,” “CDI,” “fecal microbiota transplantation,” “FMT,” “live biotherapeutic product,” “pediatric,” “children,” and “recurrent.” Reference lists of identified articles were reviewed for additional relevant studies. The inclusion criteria encompassed clinical trials, cohort studies, case series, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guidelines pertaining to pediatric CDI or FMT in children. Studies exclusively in adults were included where pediatric data were absent or to provide contextual comparison.

[Clostridioides difficile infection in children]
Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is a gram-positive anaerobic bacterium that produces highly resistant spores that are transmitted via the fecal-oral route and can persist in healthcare and community environments, leading to widespread infections. 4 , 5 CDI produces a wide clinical spectrum ranging from mild diarrhea to severe hemorrhagic colitis, with potentially life-threatening complications, including toxic megacolon and death. 4 , 6 Antibiotic use, increasing age, and underlying comorbidities that promote gut dysbiosis all heighten susceptibility.
CDI rates rose dramatically from the 1990s in both adults and children, emerging as a global public health threat. 7 CDI was initially considered a predominantly healthcare associated (HA) illness, however a large U.S. study demonstrated a significant decrease from 7.09 HA-CDI pediatric cases per 10,000 patient days in 2013 to 4.89 cases per 10,000 patient-days in 2019 while community acquired (CA) CDI rates increased from 9.6/100,000 children per year in 2012 to peak at 16.9/100,000 children per year in 2015. 8 , 9 Subsequently, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Emerging Infections Program confirmed that the incidence of CA-CDI surpassed HA-CDI across all age groups, including children ages 1–17 y old where the incidence of CA-CDI is 21/100,000 persons and HA-CDI is 8.1/100,000 persons. 10 This shift likely reflects the adoption of robust infection control and antimicrobial stewardship measures in healthcare settings. 11 , 12
The most common risk factor for CDI in children is antibiotic exposure, particularly with clindamycin, third-generation cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones. 13 , 14 Although most children with CDI report antibiotic exposure in the preceding 4 weeks, many have no prior antibiotic exposure, especially among those with CA-CDI. 15 Additionally, multiple courses of antibiotics further increase the risk of CDI (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.25–2.97). 16 Acid suppressants, specifically proton pump inhibitors, also increase CDI risk, likely through their effects on the gut microbiome. 14 , 16 , 17 Prior hospitalization, length of hospitalization, and even recent outpatient visits are additional risk factors, underscoring the ongoing importance of infection control in pediatric settings. 14 Approximately 30%–50% of children who develop CDI have significant underlying comorbidities, including prior solid organ transplantation, immunodeficiency, malignancy, and inflammatory bowel d

[Current non-FMT treatment options]
The first step in management, regardless of the therapeutic agent being used, is discontinuation of the inciting antibiotic when able. Pediatric treatment guidelines from 2017 recommend that first-line antibiotic therapy for non-severe initial CDI or first recurrence in children includes oral metronidazole (7.5 mg/kg/dose three or four times daily for 10 d) or oral vancomycin (10 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 10 d). 34 A systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric observational studies demonstrated significantly lower cure rates with metronidazole compared to vancomycin, consistent with adult data, and has driven increasing use of vancomycin in pediatric practice. 8 , 43 Metronidazole has been progressively de-prioritized in both adult and pediatric practice owing to inferior efficacy, increasing clinical failure rates, and palatability challenges from its metallic taste; its use is now generally discouraged except where access to alternatives is limited. For severe initial CDI, oral or rectal vancomycin, with or without intravenous metronidazole (10 mg/kg/dose three times daily), is recommended. For second or subsequent recurrences, recommended regimens include a tapered and pulsed vancomycin course over at least 6 weeks or vancomycin for 10 d followed by rifaximin for 20 d, with FMT as an alternative. 34 A shared limitation of these regimens is their frequent dosing, which has been consistently associated with reduced medication adherence. 44
While the 2021 adult CDI guidelines recommend fidaxomicin as first-line therapy for initial or rCDI, the pediatric IDSA/SHEA guidelines, last updated in 2017, do not yet reflect this recommendation. 34 , 45 However, compelling pediatric data exist. The SUNSHINE trial, a phase 3, multicenter RCT, compared fidaxomicin (oral suspension 16 mg/kg/dose twice daily for children under 6 y, or 200 mg tablets twice daily for older children) to vancomycin for 10 d in patients under 18 y of age. 46 Fidaxomicin demonstrated significantly higher rates of global cure, i.e., confirmed clinical response without rCDI until the time of assessment. A real-world, retrospective pediatric multicenter study supports these findings, showing that fidaxomicin is well-tolerated with a 78.5% cure rate without relapse at day 60. 47 Fidaxomicin’s twice-daily dosing and lower rCDI rate also make it an appealing option. [Rationale for FMT in pediatric CDI]
Gut dysbiosis plays a central role in CDI pathogenesis. Disruption of the commensal gut microbiota, most commonly by antibiotic exposure, permits CD colonization, proliferation, and toxin production. Despite a small number of effective treatments, rCDI is a common challenge in children, necessitating the need for FMT. 37-40
FMT is defined as the transfer of fecal material from a healthy screened donor into a patient with rCDI, with the goal of restoring microbial diversity and re-establishing colonization resistance against CD. 57 While the exact mechanism of clearance of C. difficile through FMT remains unclear, observed microbiome changes include: (1) relative increase in abundance of Bacteroidetes and decreased abundance of Proteobacteria; (2) increased diversity of the microbial communities; (3) post-FMT similarities between the patients’ microbiome and the donor flora; and (4) restoration of normal fecal bile acid composition. 58-60 FMT is now considered the standard of care for patients with rCDI non-responsive to antibiotics. 61
FMT was first described in the English literature in 1958 in adults with pseudomembranous enterocolitis. 62 The landmark RCT by van Nood et al. in 2013 demonstrated FMT superiority over vancomycin for rCDI (81% vs. 31% cure rate), 59 and numerous subsequent RCTs, observational studies, and registry data have confirmed FMT efficacy in adults with cure rates exceeding 90%. 1 , 63-67 The first reported pediatric FMT via nasogastric tube was in 2010, and the first colonoscopic FMT in a child was in 2012. 68 , 69
FMT for Recurrent CDI: The primary and best-evidenced indication for FMT in children is prevention of further episodes in those with rCDI – defined as two or more recurrences after an initial treated episode. The rationale is the restoration of gut microbial diversity and colonization resistance, disrupted by repeated antibiotic courses as per adults. Large pediatric cohorts confirm cure rates exceeding 80% for this indication, as discussed in detail below. 3 RCTs are not available in children.
FMT for severe, fulminant, or refractory CDI: FMT has also been used as rescue therapy in children with severe or fulminant CDI unresponsive to antibiotics, or in those with refractory disease. Evidence for this indication in children is limited to case reports and small series. 70 The physiologic rationale –rapid microbiome reconstitution to interrupt toxin-mediated colonic injury and potentially the immune-modulating effect of F

[Effectiveness and safety of FMT in pediatric CDI]
To date, no prospective RCTs have evaluated the use of FMT in children with CDI, representing a significant gap in the evidence base. Current evidence is limited to retrospective studies and single-center cohort studies (Table 1).

candidates.abstract: Background The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 Results We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected. Video Abstract.

[Introduction]
Across all environments, microbes help sustain ecosystems by exchanging and transforming key elements such as nitrogen [31], carbon, and sulfur [65, 73], generating energy through chemo- or phototrophic metabolisms, and recycling nutrients. Consequently, microbes directly shape their environments by altering nutrient availability, and the composition and redox structure of the Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) comprising the exometabolome [45, 67, 77]. In turn, microbial community composition and function are shaped by physicochemical conditions, including pH, oxygen availability, nutrient supply, and hydrodynamic connectivity [69], leading to a bidirectional relationship where each impacts the other. Comprehensive multi-omics studies, integrating metagenomics, metabolomics, and environmental measurements, are needed to resolve the intricate biogeochemical connections that shape the microbiome [31, 57, 79, 81]. Such multi-omics studies have been made possible the development of untargeted high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry of metabolomes [11] with advanced data processing tools [15, 27] and high-throughput metagenome shotgun sequencing [36, 38, 58] followed by de novo assembly and functional annotation [70]. These advances allow for increasingly detailed characterizations of potential microbe-metabolite interactions [42]. Despite these technological advances, the application of fully integrated multi-omics approaches in natural systems remains limited as the high complexity and natural variability of these systems introduce challenges that are largely absent from laboratory-based experiments [59]. Naturally stratified or physically isolated systems provide valuable opportunities to overcome some of these challenges by offering stable gradients over relatively small spatial scales [26]. Marine sinkholes can thus function as natural laboratories, as they often host sharp biogeochemical transitions.
Here, we characterize the microbial ecology of the northern sinkholes in the Luymes Bank, located at the northeast margin of the Saba Bank in the Caribbean Sea. Several of these sinkholes were previously described by Humphreys et al. [30], characterizing their complex geological origins and physical structure. Notably, Humphreys et al. [30] described an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 < 60 µmol/kg) submerged ‘lake’ starting at a depth of 220 m within the sinkhole with the deepest bottom depth (306 m). This unusual environment is thought to originate from the

[Methods]
We collected a total of 59 paired metagenomic and metabolomic samples from 21 stations on the Luymes Bank near Saba in December 2019 (Fig. 1A). Water chemistry parameters were measured as described by [30] (Supplementary Methods, Supplementary Table S3). Based on these parameters samples were clustered using Ward’s minimal variance clustering into six environments as follows: surface (n = 16), platform (n = 12), shallow sinkhole (n = 14), deep sinkhole (n = 9), acid lake (n = 6), and mesopelagic (n = 2). More detailed information on sample collection and storage can be found in the Supplementary methods.
Characterization of the environment: A map of Luymes Bank and integrated sinkholes (modified from Humphreys et al. 2022). B Ward’s minimal variance clustering of physicochemical parameters; rows correspond to samples and are annotated by the six defined environmental clusters (surface (n = 16), platform (n = 12), shallow sinkhole (n = 14), deep sinkhole (n = 9), acid lake (n = 6), and mesopelagic (n = 2)). Before clustering all nutrients were log10 transformed and all factors were normalized using z-scores. C Sampling depths of samples grouped by sinkhole and area (FS = far south, E = east, S = south, W = west, N = north, and O = open ocean). Colored by environmental cluster, see B. D Boxplots of measured physicochemical parameters grouped and colored by environmental cluster, see legend in B
Flow cytometric enumeration of prokaryotes (including bacteria and archaea) and viruses was performed at the NIOZ according to the protocol by Brussaard et al. [6] and using a TE buffer at pH 8.2. Samples were diluted in TE buffer and stained with the nucleic acid-specific green fluorescence dye SYBRGreen-I (10–5 dilution of commercial stock, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 15 min at room temperature for prokaryotes and for 10 min at 80 °C for viruses. Samples were then analyzed using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer with a 488 nm laser (BD Biosciences, USA).
Total DNA was extracted from seawater using the NucleoSpin Tissue DNA extraction kit following manufacturer instructions with some small adjustments (see supplementary methods section: “DNA isolation”). The isolated DNA was measured using the Denovix DS-11, and ranged from 1.7 to 12 ng/µL. Genomic DNA libraries were subsequently prepared using the TruSeq DNA Nano LT Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina), whereby DNA was mechanically fragmented, end-repaired and 3′-adenylated, ligated to indexed adapters, size-selected by bead-ba

[Results]
The Luymes Banks consist of a carbonate platform raised from the ocean floor, up to a depth of 60–80 m below the ocean surface and features multiple sinkholes with depths of up to 475 m below the ocean surface across their 66 km2 area [71]. We performed a characterization of seven of these sinkholes and adjacent open-ocean stations using multivariate clustering of hydrographic and biogeochemical parameters (phosphate, nitrate, nitrite, pH, depth, dissolved oxygen, transmissivity, salinity, and chlorophyll,(Fig. 1B, C). We excluded total alkalinity from the clustering analysis due to its strong collinearity with dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC, Supplementary Fig. S3). The multivariate clustering revealed six distinct environments: surface, platform, shallow sinkhole, deep sinkhole, acid lake, and mesopelagic (Fig. 1 C, D). Each cluster delineates a discrete physicochemical biome characterized by a unique combination of water column properties (Supplementary Fig. S3B), that approximately correspond to increasing depths (surface: n = 16, mean = 2.7 m, std = 3 m; platform: n = 12, mean = 70 m, std = 6 m, shallow sinkhole: n = 14, mean = 92 m, std = 10 m; deep sinkhole: n = 9, mean = 177 m, std = 47 m; acid lake: n = 6, mean = 275 m, std = 30 m; and mesopelagic: n = 2, mean = 536 m, std = 76 m). With the notable exception of the acid lake, the six different environments correspond to regular oceanographic patterns including higher nutrient levels in deeper, cooler water, and a chlorophyll max at intermediate depth [12, 40]. Samples collected near the surface (surface) were similar across all sinkholes and the open ocean, featuring high light, temperature, and dissolved oxygen with low concentrations of salinity, inorganic nutrients, and chlorophyll (Fig. 1C, D, E). Samples collected just above the platform depth at a depth of 60–80 m (platform), had higher salinity (mean = 37 ppt,std = 0.18 ppt) than the surface samples (mean = 34.7 ppt; std = 0.27 ppt), the highest chlorophyll concentrations of all environments (mean = 0.31 µg/kg, std = 0.03 µg/kg), and marginal increases in oxygen (+ 0.3 µmol/kg), nitrate (+ 0.11 µmol/kg), and nitrite (+ 0.035 µmol/kg) relative to the surface. The conditions within the sinkholes (shallow sinkhole, deep sinkhole, and acid lake) diverged from platform waters with increased salinity, nitrate, and phosphate. These patterns were consistent across both northern and southern sinkholes. The most striking deviations from the general p

[Discussion]
Exploring remote habitats has become more accessible thanks to large-scale omics datasets reducing the reliance on laboratory conditions. Yet these environments pose analytical challenges that differ markedly from those encountered in well-characterized or laboratory-controlled systems. A key difficulty lies in the holistic treatment of each sample: all detected metabolites and microbial taxa are jointly associated with the same environmental context, and consequently with one another. This obscures the directionality of causal relationships, as most conclusions are limited to co-occurrences, and our current analysis is primarily correlative. This limitation means that a mechanistic explanation is currently impossible to provide, based on the correlation network alone. Instead, the identified connections should be viewed as hypothesis-generating leads that warrant targeted validation through experiments or modeling. It is also reasonable to expect that aspects of microbial adaptation involve transcriptional changes or protein-level modifications and therefore are not captured in the functional abundance analysis. Further analysis such as protein sequence comparisons or RNA sequencing is likely to reveal additional fascinating insights within this ecosystem, if such data becomes available.
We can contemplate how our results relate to future ocean acidification. Laboratory studies report reduced nitrification rates under acidified conditions [5], yet the acid lake demonstrates that key nitrogen-cycling lineages can persist at pH levels of ~ 6 far below end-century surface ocean projections (~ 7.7–7.8). This suggests that at least some nitrifying archaea and bacteria possess sufficient plasticity to maintain function under chronic acidification. Cyanobacteria, which were still present at a low relative abundance within the nearly aphotic deep sinkholes (mean = 0.03, SD = 0.016), were almost completely lost in the acid lake (mean = 0.0017, SD = 0.0002), suggesting that, even when taking into account the low light conditions, photosynthetic primary producers may be more vulnerable to combined acidification and deoxygenation. Naturally, we should be careful with our interpretations, as the acid lake is nearly aphotic, higher in dissolved inorganic carbon and other nutrients, and resembles a chronically stressed, hydrodynamically isolated endpoint rather than the gradual transition expected in the open ocean,

candidates.title: Polaris: A toolkit for standardized construction, integration, and quantitative testing in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
candidates.abstract: Existing synthetic biology toolkits have expanded part libraries and assembly capabilities. However, new users may still encounter ambiguity in construct definitions, hierarchical transitions, genomic integration routes, and quantitative testing procedures. Here, we present Polaris, a Golden Gate toolkit for Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Polaris uses a MoClo-derived three-level hierarchy. Level 1 stores reusable parts, Level 2 generates transcription units and other intermediate constructs, and Level 3 supports multigene assembly and switching between testing and integration backbones. The toolkit distinguishes part interfaces from transcription unit interfaces, uses BpiI and BsaI in successive assembly stages, and provides parallel ccdB and mScarletI3 screening options. Integration modules and quantitative characterization frameworks were implemented in both hosts and demonstrated using representative genetic parts and activation and repression systems. A companion digital platform further encodes the Level 1 to Level 3 rules for assembly planning. Polaris connects hierarchical construction, stable genetic implementation, and quantitative testing within a common execution framework, providing a practical basis for data accumulation, part standardization, and future automation.

candidates.title: Cyborg bacteria as semi-living organelles for the augmentation of mammalian cells.
candidates.abstract: Synthetic organelles are engineered to replicate the compartmentalization and dynamic functionality of natural organelles, offering the potential to reprogram or rescue cellular functions. Existing approaches, such as protein cages, biomolecular condensates, and other artificial compartments, have shown promise but remain limited by their capacity to perform multifunctional tasks. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Cyborg Bacterial Organelles (CBOs), which are non-replicating, metabolically active bacteria engineered to function as living synthetic organelles within mammalian cells. Unlike synthetic systems or replicating endosymbionts, CBOs integrate the biological complexity of living organisms with the stability and tunability of engineered materials. CBOs are generated by permeating bacteria with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEG) based monomers followed by intracellular UV induced hydrogel crosslinking, producing a structurally reinforced, non-replicative chassis capable of sustained activity inside host cells. Here, we show that CBOs remained detectable inside mammalian cells with substantially reduced morphological disruption compared with wild-type bacteria. Furthermore, we show that CBOs can perform complex functions intracellularly, including responses to extracellular chemical stimuli via synthetic gene circuits and execution of enzymatic reactions such as prodrug conversion into a therapeutic drug. Notably, we also show that CBOs protect host cells from chemically induced mitochondrial stress. Transcriptomic analysis revealed host gene expression changes associated with membrane remodeling, ion transport, and metabolic buffering, suggesting that CBOs modulate the host in protective and adaptive ways. Together, these findings establish CBOs as a novel hybrid material platform for intracellular engineering while addressing key limitations of current synthetic organelle systems. CBOs open new possibilities for cellular modulation in therapeutic and diagnostic applications.

candidates.title: Dysregulated microbiota-gut-brain axis induced by intermittent access to palatable food is associated with binge-like eating regardless of obesity development.
candidates.abstract: Recurrent consumption of energy dense palatable foods contributes to the rising prevalence of obesity and can also promote loss-of-control eating in a subset of individuals. Obesity is commonly associated with peripheral inflammation, impaired sensitivity to appetite-regulating hormones, and alterations in gut microbiota composition, all of which may exacerbate binge-eating behaviors. However, emerging evidence suggests that repeated exposure to palatable foods alone can induce maladaptive eating patterns even prior to the development of obesity. In this study, intermittent access to palatable food (e.g., cheesecake) induced binge-like eating behavior in non-obese female rats, accompanied by hypothalamic microglial reactivity and altered leptin signaling pathway. Additionally, even sporadic exposure to palatable food was sufficient to alter gut microbiota composition, increasing microbial diversity and promoting taxa adapted to high fat and sugar availability, including potential pathobionts (e.g., Escherichia, Streptococcus, and Clostridium spp.) as well as carbohydrate-fermenting bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Roseburia . Notably, increased microbial diversity was associated with both hyperphagic behavior and reduced hypothalamic leptin pathway responsiveness. Overall, these findings suggest that gut microbiota imbalance and central neuroimmune adaptations occurred in the absence of significant weight gain. This highlights the potential value of early interventions which may represent promising candidate strategies for future investigation.

[Introduction]
Loss-of-control eating, defined as recurrent episodes of binge eating, has long been reported as a pathological eating behavior observed in bulimia nervosa (BN) and binge-eating disorder (BED). 1-4 Compulsive eaters report frequent episodes of consuming large quantities of appetizing foods beyond the satiety threshold, losing control over their eating and experiencing remorse after overeating. Despite somatic and mental aversive consequences, these individuals are unsuccessful in giving up binge eating. 5
Unlike BN, BED does not include compensatory purging actions like vomiting, intense physical activity or excessive dieting, 6 which partially explains its strong association with obesity. Recent evidence suggests that visceral adipose expansion releases fatty acids promoting insulin resistance, increases adipokines such as leptin, and secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines leading to low-grade peripheral inflammation. 7 Hence, abdominal obesity may trigger central inflammation, impair satiety signaling and promote overeating. 8
Meanwhile, multiple studies have reported that autoimmune and inflammatory diseases are associated with increased risk for developing BN and BED, one striking observation being that childhood diagnosis of an autoimmune or autoinflammatory disease increased the risk of developing BN by 73%. 9-11 And although its prevalence clearly increases with excessive weight gain, BED occurs in persons across the weight spectrum, 3 , 12 underscoring the fact that overeating is also reported in the absence of or before the onset of obesity. Preclinical evidence confirms bingeing behaviors in rodents consuming palatable foods weeks before the onset of weight gain, 13 , 14 concomitant with central inflammation 15 and altered gut microbiota composition. 16 , 17 Intermittent binge eating has greater adverse metabolic consequences than the chronic overeating of smaller but more frequent meals, and this chronic binging may compromise immune function. 18 It is well known that central inflammation contributes to overeating by disrupting the signaling cascade of hormones regulating appetite control within hypothalamic regions involved in food intake regulation. 19 The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) and arcuate nucleus (ARC) play a pivotal role in the integration of homeostatic and hedonic signals driving eating behavior 20 , 21 and increased levels of proinflammatory factors in these brain regions, among which various cytokines including IL-1, IFN-γ, TNF-α 

[Materials and methods]
Thirty-five 6-week-old Wistar Han female rats (weighing 174.11 g ± 3.38 at the beginning of the experiment) were used in this study. The rats were bred in our animal facility from breeding pairs obtained from Charles River Laboratories (France) and were maintained under conventional health conditions. All animals were kept under a 12-h light/dark cycle (light off at 9 am) in temperature- and humidity-controlled room. Food and water were provided ad libitum and all manipulations (animal weighing, change of diet, stool collection) were done during the dark phase of the light cycle. The entire experiment was carried out in agreement with the Swiss Cantonal Veterinary Office and the Committee for animal experimentation (authorization VD3047.1). Animals were monitored daily for body condition, general appearance and signs of pain or distress. No unexpected adverse events occurred during the study. Rats were block-randomized into the C/C and C/P groups by an experimenter blinded to subsequent behavioral outcomes, matched for baseline body weight and food intake. Within each diet group, animals were further randomly and blindly pre-assigned, prior to the start of the intermittent feeding protocol, to one of two terminal-procedure sub-cohorts: (i) decapitation with trunk-blood and fecal collection (used for microbiota, SCFA, serum inflammatory markers, and qPCR gene expression), or (ii) transcardiac perfusion (used for microglial morphology study). These two endpoints are mutually exclusive at the tissue level (perfusion-fixation precludes serum collection and optimal RNA extraction, while decapitation precludes optimal fixation for high-resolution immunohistochemistry). Consequently, these analyses were performed in separate, non-overlapping sub-cohorts of animals rather than using different tissues from the same animals.
No animals were excluded from the study after allocation. Analysis-specific exclusions resulting from unavailable or insufficient samples are reported together with the final sample size for each outcome. Whenever feasible, sample processing, image acquisition, outcome quantification and statistical analysis were performed blindly.
6-week-old rats were individually housed (in type III cages 425 × 266 × 185 mm containing a wooden arch and nesting material as enrichment) and after ten days of acclimatization they were split in two groups of equal food intake: 17 of them were assigned to the control C/C (chow/chow) group and received standard chow 

[Results]
Control C/C rats maintained stable daily intake throughout the eight-week protocol (Figure 2A). In contrast, C/P rats consumed more calories during cheesecake access and less chow after returning to the chow-only phase, with the reduction in chow intake becoming apparent from week 3 (Figure 2B). Over the full protocol, cumulative caloric intake was higher in C/P than in C/C (C/C: 3 141 ± 62 kcal; C/P: 3 363 ± 56.6 kcal; t = 2.643, P = 0.0125), whereas body-weight trajectories did not differ between groups (Figure 2C). The cumulative values shown in Figure 2A and B cover the complete 48-h access period, whereas Figure 2D reports intake during the first 6 h of the first access day.
To assess binge-like eating, food intake was recorded every two hours (from 0 h to 6 h after cheesecake availability) on the first day of cheesecake access during week 1 and week 8. In week 1, both groups ingested a similar proportion of daily calories in the first two-hour interval (C/C: 14.2% ± 6.1%; C/P: 10.3% ± 8.8%). By week 8, C/P rats consumed 28.8% of their daily calories within the first two hours of cheesecake availability, indicative of pronounced binge-like eating compared both to the control group and to their intake during the first week of exposure (Figure 2D), as confirmed by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (Time × Group: F(5,165) = 10.56, P < 0.0001; Time: F(3.965, 130.8) = 5.3, P = 0.0006; Group: F(1,33) = 8.284, P = 0.007). Intermediate 2-h intake measurements were not collected during weeks 2–7, by design, to minimize handling-related disturbance across the full 8-week protocol; the trajectory of binge-phenotype emergence between week 1 and week 8 therefore cannot be further resolved with the present dataset, and finer-grained temporal sampling is recommended in future studies.

(B) Food intake of C/C and C/P rats by phase. C/P rats exhibit increased food intake when fed cheesecake and a progressive reduction in food intake when returned to standard chow (C/C n = 17, C/P n = 18; 2-way repeated measure ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparison; *p < 0.05). Effect of intermittent feeding protocol on body weight: (C) body weight of C/C and C/P rats during the entire experiment. No difference in body weight was observed between the two groups. [Discussion]
The microbiota–gut–brain axis has emerged as a promising conceptual framework for understanding binge eating disorder pathophysiology, extending classical models that view eating disorders primarily through psychological or behavioral lenses. 35 , 36 , 74 , 75 This study provides converging evidence that intermittent access to palatable food triggers a sequence of biological changes through complex neuroinflammatory pathways and modified leptin signaling mechanisms, thereby creating a self-perpetuating cycle of disordered eating behavior that occurs independently of body weight changes. These findings provide a basis for generating hypotheses regarding potential therapeutic targets and preventive strategies, although their clinical relevance remains to be established.
Binge-eating behaviors and related eating disorders are substantially more prevalent in females, both in humans and animal models, 76 , 77 supporting a biological basis for sex-specific vulnerability. In addition, sex differences in gut microbiota composition, neuroimmune signaling, and microbiota–brain interactions are increasingly recognized. 78 Hormonal, metabolic, and immune-related differences between sexes may therefore influence microbiota composition, SCFA production, and hypothalamic inflammatory responses. Consequently, the findings reported here in females may not directly generalize to males, and future studies including both sexes will be necessary to evaluate sex-specific microbiota–brain mechanisms involved in binge-eating behavior. Rats were housed individually to accurately measure per-animal food intake, a requirement for the primary behavioral endpoint. Although this may induce chronic stress, its equal application to C/C and C/P groups cannot explain between-group differences.
Our central finding is that brief, intermittent exposure to palatable food (only two consecutive days per week for eight weeks) substantially alters gut bacterial composition and functional products, potentially affecting brain function and feeding behavior. The microbiota shifted consistently, with enrichment of Bifidobacterium, Streptococcus, Roseburia, and Eubacterium alongside depletion of Alistipes and Prevotella. This pattern resembles chronic Western diet-induced remodeling, 79 , 80 suggesting that even brief, intermittent consumption of palatable food can induce microbiological changes. candidates.title: ESCRT-III assembly restores membrane tension in micron-scale plasma membrane repair.
candidates.abstract: Plasma membrane integrity is essential for cellular survival, yet how cells repair micron-scale plasma membrane ruptures remains poorly understood. Here, using the genetically tractable Caenorhabditis elegans epidermis, we combine live imaging, genetics, super-resolution microscopy, and biophysical approaches to define a size-dependent role for endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT)-III in large-scale membrane repair. Small wounds induce transient, focal VPS-32 accumulation, whereas large wounds trigger the formation of a persistent but dynamic, circumferential ESCRT-III assembly that remains associated with the wound during repair. Formation of this assembly requires conserved ESCRT regulators, including ALX-1, TSG-101, and VPS-4, together with VPS-32 polymerization. The wound-associated ESCRT-III assembly is required for membrane tension restoration and efficient membrane repair, while disrupting VPS-32 polymerization impairs tension recovery, reduces vesicle recruitment and wound closure, and consequently compromises axon regeneration and organismal survival following injury. Together, our findings suggest that large plasma membrane wounds induce a persistent, dynamic ESCRT-III assembly that restores membrane tension and facilitates vesicle-mediated membrane addition to promote wound repair.

candidates.title: An engineered probiotic yeast converts extracellular ATP into adenosine to alleviate experimental colitis.
candidates.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic relapsing intestinal disorder characterized by mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, and gut microbial dysbiosis. Excessive extracellular ATP (eATP) accumulates in inflamed intestinal tissues and amplifies immune activation through purinergic signaling, whereas adenosine generated from extracellular nucleotide metabolism exerts immunoregulatory effects. Here, we engineered the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii to sense eATP and convert it into adenosine through a CRISPR-engineered dual-enzyme pathway consisting of apyrase and 5'-nucleotidase. The engineered strain showed ATP-responsive pathway activation and efficiently generated adenosine from eATP, allowing extracellular nucleotide metabolism to be modulated in inflammatory settings. Oral administration of this strain significantly alleviated disease severity in acute dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and showed beneficial effects in a repeated-DSS model, improved barrier-related epithelial features, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and supported mucosal recovery. Integrated microbiome and transcriptome analyses further showed partial restoration of gut microbial community structure, partial recovery of predicted microbial purine-related pathways, and attenuation of mucosal T-cell activation. Together, these findings indicate that engineered Saccharomyces boulardii can regulate extracellular purine metabolism in the inflamed gut and provide a microbial strategy for modulating intestinal inflammation.

candidates.title: From community profiling to functional insights: bacterial populations in marine sediments from an Antarctic Specially Protected Area (Terra Nova Bay, Ross Sea, Antarctica).
candidates.abstract: Marine sediments remain among the least characterised components of the Antarctic microbial landscape. Here, bacterial communities were investigated in sediments from three sites within the Antarctic Specially Protected Area No. 161, in Terra Nova Bay (Ross Sea, Antarctica). Samples were collected during the XXXIII Italian Antarctic Expedition. The sites differed in their local environmental context, including proximity to the Adélie penguin colony and Mario Zucchelli Station. Bacterial communities were characterised by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region), with amplicon sequence variants resolved using DADA2, and complemented by PICRUSt2 predicted functional potential, bacterial isolation, and quorum-sensing bioassays. Bacteroidota and Proteobacteria dominated all sites, but community composition and diversity differed significantly among sampling sites. AC showed the highest alpha diversity, while ASPA2 showed the lowest. Of the 5423 amplicon sequence variants detected across the nine samples (three per site), 680 were shared across all samples and defined a core microbiome dominated by Bacteroidota and Proteobacteria. Despite marked differences in community composition, broad predicted functional profiles were relatively conserved, whereas finer-scale KEGG Orthology profiles showed site-associated variation. Seventeen psychrophilic strains were isolated, predominantly Psychrobacter, and most displayed hydrolytic activity towards olive oil, tributyrin, or both substrates. Biosensor-responsive activity was detected exclusively in enrichment cultures and not in extracts from individual isolates, providing preliminary evidence of putative quorum-sensing-related activity associated with mixed microbial consortia. These findings provide a baseline for investigating environmental drivers of Antarctic sediment microbiomes and microbial interactions in future studies.

candidates.title: Genetic and environmental predictors of seasonality and seasonal affective disorder in individuals with depression.
candidates.abstract: The etiology and nosological status of seasonal affective disorder (SAD) as a specifier of depressive episodes versus a transdiagnostic disorder are the subject of debate. In this study, we investigated the underlying etiology of SAD and dimensional seasonality by examining their association with latitude and genetic risk for a range of traits, and investigated gene-environment interactions. This study included 12,460 adults (76% female, aged 18-90) with a history of depression from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Regression models included predictors for latitude (distance from equator) and polygenic scores for eight traits: major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, anxiety disorders, chronotype, sleep duration, body mass index, vitamin D levels, and educational attainment. Outcomes were SAD status and general seasonality score. SAD was positively associated with latitude (OR[95%CI] = 1.05[1.03-1.06], padjusted < 0.001), and there was nominal evidence of additive and multiplicative interactions between chronotype genetic risk and latitude (β = -0.0014[-0.0024,-0.0003], padjusted = 0.122; OR = 0.98[0.97-1.00], padjusted = 0.122). General seasonality score was associated with latitude (IRR = 1.01[1.01-1.01], padjusted < 0.001) and genetic risk for major depressive disorder (IRR =1.03[1.02-1.04], padjusted < 0.001), bipolar disorder (IRR = 1.02[1.01-1.03], padjusted = 0.001), anxiety disorders (IRR = 1.03[1.01-1.04], padjusted < 0.001), vitamin D levels (OR = 0.89[0.83-0.96], padjusted = 0.048), and educational attainment (IRR = 0.97[0.96-0.98], padjusted < 0.001). These findings enhance understanding of SAD etiology, highlighting contributions of psychiatric genetic risk and geographic measures on seasonal behavior, and support examining seasonality as a continuous dimension.

candidates.title: Characterizing hypertension in activated PI3K delta syndrome: Findings from Epic Cosmos.
candidates.abstract: APDS is a rare inborn error of immunity with comorbidity patterns that have yet to be characterized at a large scale. Using Epic Cosmos, a de-identified electronic health record database, we conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of 866 patients identified by structured diagnosis codes (ICD-10: D84.81; SNOMED: 793412000). Findings revealed that hypertension was coded as affecting 28.5% of the cohort, with age-stratified analyses demonstrating higher prevalence among younger APDS patients compared with age-matched non-APDS peers. Among patients aged ≤50 years, hypertension prevalence was 24.05% in the APDS group compared with 10.89% in the age-matched non-APDS population (prevalence ratio 2.21, 95% CI, 1.90-2.57, P < 0.0001). This association remained prominent in a more specific APDS sensitivity cohort in which the base population required an APDS diagnosis, alongside an allergy and immunology encounter. The findings of this paper provide large-scale characterization of APDS and identify hypertension, particularly among younger APDS patients, as a potentially underrecognized comorbidity that warrants further investigation.
